questions.question: What is the difference between == and === in JavaScript?
questions.title: == vs === in JavaScript — Type Coercion Explained
questions.direct_answer:
What is the difference between == and === in JavaScript?

**In one line:** name the mechanism, where it applies (the type checker, emit pipeline, and how types line up with runtime JS), and the user-visible outcome.

**Interviewers dig into:** Strict (===) vs abstract (==) equality; type coercion rules for ==; why === is preferred.

**Classic weak answer:** Saying == always does 'smart' conversion — the coercion rules have surprising cases (e.g. [] == false is true).

**Senior finish:** Show famous quirks: null == undefined (true), NaN !== NaN, [] == ![] (true); mention Object.is for NaN/±0 cases.

sections.title: Why this question matters
sections.content:
This question — **== vs === in JavaScript — Type Coercion Explained** — shows up constantly in **frontend / fullstack** interviews because it separates candidates who memorized docs from candidates who can **reason about real systems**.

**Restate the prompt:** What is the difference between == and === in JavaScript?

A gold-level answer does four things in order:

1. **Define** the terms in plain English (what it is / what problem it solves).
2. **Explain the mechanism** (what runs when: browser, bundler, framework, network).
3. **Compare trade-offs** (speed vs correctness vs security vs DX) with **when you would not use** the default.
4. **Ground it in production** — caching, auth, observability, tests, or an incident you handled.

Interviewers are listening for: **Strict (===) vs abstract (==) equality; type coercion rules for ==; why === is preferred**.

The fastest way to lose points is: **Saying == always does 'smart' conversion — the coercion rules have surprising cases (e.g. [] == false is true)**.

If you only add one “senior” layer, make it: **Show famous quirks: null == undefined (true), NaN !== NaN, [] == ![] (true); mention Object.is for NaN/±0 cases**.

sections.title: Deep dive — what to say
sections.content:
### What to explain (middle of the answer)

- **Core mechanics:** Strict (===) vs abstract (==) equality; type coercion rules for ==; why === is preferred
- **Concrete shape:** give a small code or config snippet *only if it clarifies* (5–15 lines max).
- **Interviewer follow-ups:** expect “what breaks in production?”, “how do you debug?”, “what would you measure?” — answer them proactively.

### How to sound senior (without rambling)

- Tie the feature to **user-visible outcomes** (performance, accessibility, security).
- Mention **one failure mode** you have actually seen (race, stale cache, hydration mismatch, flaky test).
- Close with **one decision rule** (“choose X when …; choose Y when …”).

sections.title: Trade-offs & senior signal
sections.content:
### Trade-offs interviewers expect you to name

- **Speed vs safety** (types, runtime checks, validation).
- **DX vs constraints** (framework magic vs explicit wiring).
- **SEO / first paint vs interactivity** (SSR/SSG/CSR choices where relevant).
- **Security vs convenience** (tokens, cookies, localStorage, third-party scripts).

### What “book answer” misses

- **Book answer:** repeats definitions.
- **Strong answer:** names **saying == always does 'smart' conversion — the coercion rules have surprising cases (e.g. [] == false is true)** and what you do instead.

**Pitfall (15 seconds):** Call out **Saying == always does 'smart' conversion — the coercion rules have surprising cases (e.g. [] == false is true)** — interviewers reward honesty about real bugs.

questions.question: What is the difference between null and undefined in JavaScript?
questions.title: null vs undefined in JavaScript — Differences and When to Use Each
questions.direct_answer:
What is the difference between null and undefined in JavaScript?

**In one line:** name the mechanism, where it applies (the type checker, emit pipeline, and how types line up with runtime JS), and the user-visible outcome.

**Interviewers dig into:** undefined is the default for uninitialized variables; null is an intentional empty value; typeof differences; JSON serialization behavior.

**Classic weak answer:** Saying null and undefined are the same — they are equal with == but not ===; and typeof returns different strings.

**Senior finish:** Note typeof null === 'object' (historic bug), JSON.stringify drops undefined but keeps null, and optional chaining returns undefined not null.
